images.text:
Adam: Wow, this looks great! You really thought of everything! This is a really great venue.
Kristi: Thanks! It has been a lot of work, but I'm happy with how it's turned out so far. I'm nervous though. We still have a lot to set up and things could still go awry.
Adam: Like what?
Kristi: Well, my biggest fear is that no one will show up. I have invited a lot of people, but it is possible that no one will come. Maybe I should have invited more of my friends and family. At least I know they would come for sure.
Adam: What else are you worried about?
Kristi: Well, I have ordered food and some wine and juice. I ordered some fruit trays and veggies and dip and some cheese and crackers. I think I should have ordered some more. I guess I can always run out and get more if I need to.
Adam: How much wine have you ordered?

Kristi: Ten bottles.
Adam: Yeah, you should have ordered more.
Kristi: Adam! It's not for you! Help me set up these tables. I've planned a table for the food, a table for drinks and a table for the author to sit behind and autograph copies.
Adam: Is she going to read the book?
Kristi: Yeah, I think she is going to sit in an armchair to read and the kids can sit on the floor.
Adam: There are going to be kids here?
Kristi: Yes, Adam, it's a kids book, remember?

Adam: Oh right. So that's why you haven't ordered much wine.
Kristi: We should make sure that there's enough space for everyone. Do you think we should set up an alternate entrance? I don't want there to be a bottleneck in the entrance.
Adam: That's a good idea. There's a side door. Let's use that as an entrance too. I'll see if there's a place we can put up a sign to direct people to the entrance.
Kristi: Thanks Adam. That's really helpful. We've only got a few hours until the caterers arrive so let's get the space set up.

You use the Present Perfect tense in a variety of ways. Most commonly, it is used to show a connection between the past and the present. When you want to comment on the results of a past action that impacts the present, you use the Present Perfect Tense.
The form of the Present Perfect is:
I have invited a lot of people, but it is possible that no one will come.
You can use the Present Perfect to talk about a state that existed in the past and still exists now.
It has been a lot of work.
It has been a lot of work, but I'm happy with how it's turned out so far.
I have invited a lot of people, but it is possible that no one will come.
I have ordered food and some wine and juice.
I've planned for a table for the food, a table for drinks and a table for the author to sit behind and autograph copies.
So that's why you haven't ordered much wine.
Modals for Expressing Duty and Advice
When you want to talk about duty and advice in the present or the past, you can use the modal verbs Should or Ought to.
Should and Ought to have basically the same meaning. They are interchangeable for the most part, but should is more commonly used in North America.

We should/ought to make sure that there's enough space for everyone. (duty/responsibility)
You should invite all your friends. (advice)
You can talk about past obligations or duties by using should have and ought to have + past participle.

I think I should have ordered some more.
We ought to have made more food!
Maybe I should have invited more of my friends and family.
I think I should have ordered some more.
Yeah, you should have ordered more.
I think she ought to sit in an armchair to read and the kids can sit on the floor.
We should make sure that there's enough space for everyone.
